name: Tavi Gevinson
who_line: Style Rookie at 11, Rookie magazine founder at 15, feminist editor who taught the fashion industry to read a bedroom as criticism.
who: Tavi Gevinson started Style Rookie, a fashion blog written from her childhood bedroom in Oak Park, Illinois, at age 11. By 13 she was sitting front row at Paris couture. At 15 she founded Rookie, an online magazine for teenage girls that ran from 2011 to 2018 and became a feminist touchstone for a generation.

The New Yorker described her Christmas Eve 2008 outfit post: 'a lacy American Apparel jumpsuit, a black Rodarte top silk-screened with a skeleton, and joke-shop glasses with hologram eyeballs floating in neon liquid, worn with a deadpan face.' She took from Rei Kawakubo and the Mulleavys 'the idea that clothing can be art'.

Rookie's tagline was 'a website for teenage girls'. Its editor's letters argued that feminism was 'not a rulebook but a discussion', that you could care about clothes without dressing for men, and that 'the so-called feminine arts: beauty, glamour, style' were unfairly treated as 'dark magicks'. It was the magazine cool dairy's archive is spiritually adjacent to.
work: Style Rookie (2008–2011), the blog that made her famous. Rookie magazine (2011–2018), which she founded at 15 and edited until it closed. Acting: This Is Our Youth (2014, Broadway), Enough Said (Gillian Robespierre short), Scream (2022–2023). Writing: essays for The Cut, The New Yorker, The Believer.

In 2012 she gave a TEDxTeen talk, 'Still Figuring It Out', about how 'feminism was not a rulebook but a discussion, a place where opposing ideas could exist'. It became one of the defining statements of millennial feminism.

quotes.text: I took from Rei Kawakubo and from the Mulleavys the idea that clothing can be art, and when I was really young I took it so seriously that every day I would think of a way to comment on something.

Rookie is not your guide to Being a Teen. It is not a pamphlet on How to Be a Young Woman… Rookie is a place to make the best of the beautiful pain and cringe-worthy awkwardness of being an adolescent girl.
You can't be a feminist who's also interested in fashion. You can't care about clothes if it's not for the sake of what other people, usually men, will think of you.
I'm SHORT… adult heads do not have holes in them… I am really curious as to when news websites will write about something interesting, i.e. not what someone wore to a fashion show.
quotes.said_to: Her blog reply to 'Hatgate' (quoted by The Independent)

why_the_look: She dressed to comment on something. The Style Rookie wardrobe was 'frumpy, Grey Gardens-inspired clothes', too-big jackets, towering platforms, clusters of brooches, clear-frame Tootsie glasses, clashing prints, and ice-blue hair faded to silver. It mixed innocence with creepiness, Edward Gorey with granny brooches. At 13, at NYFW, she wore a Baggu reusable shopping bag as a hat next to Miu Miu and Christian Siriano. The high-low mix is the Rookie ethos in clothes: designer and thrift at the same level, humour as the point.
beliefs: Rei Kawakubo, Rodarte, Prada, Edward Gorey, Grey Gardens. She quoted Shulamith Firestone in Rookie editor's letters and read The Feminine Mystique in high school. She wanted feminist critique and fashion critique to be the same project.

moments.title: Style Rookie backyard self-portraits
moments.garments: Tripod self-portraits in her back garden in Oak Park: lacy American Apparel jumpsuit, black Rodarte skeleton top, joke-shop hologram glasses, turban, too-big jackets, platforms, brooches, ice-blue hair faded to silver.
moments.designer_season: American Apparel; Rodarte (per New Yorker). Starred in Rodarte's Target video (NYT).
moments.where_it_lives: The blog archive and her memory. The original Style Rookie photos are copyrighted.
moments.why_iconic: An 11-year-old taught the fashion industry to read a girl's bedroom as criticism. The look mixed innocence with creepiness on purpose, and she took from Kawakubo 'the idea that clothing can be art'. It is the DIY self-portrait as a fashion publication, the bridge from zines to blogs.

media.caption: Self-portraits by Tavi. The original blog photos are copyrighted. See New Yorker piece.

moments.title: NYFW Sept 2009 — Baggu tote as hat
moments.garments: Christian Siriano black cocktail skirt, metallic purple Miu Miu shirt, thrifted belt, vintage pearls, and a Baggu reusable shopping tote fastened with a guitar strap worn as a hat.
moments.designer_season: Christian Siriano (skirt), Miu Miu (shirt), Baggu (tote as hat), per Vanity Fair.
moments.why_iconic: At 13, at her first NYFW, she turned a grocery bag into a hat and wore it next to runway pieces. The high-low mix is pure cool dairy: designer and thrift at the same level, with humour as the point.

media.caption: Press photo. See Vanity Fair gallery.

moments.title: Dior couture 'Hatgate' — Stephen Jones bow
moments.garments: Oversized pastel-pink cartoon bow headpiece by Stephen Jones; organza Comme des Garçons coat; wallpaper-floral tights; icy-blue hair faded to grey. The season name varies by source, so it is not stated.
moments.designer_season: Stephen Jones (bow hat); Comme des Garçons (coat). No season label: sources disagree.
moments.why_iconic: 'Hatgate': Grazia's style director tweeted a photo of the couture show seen through the bow ('Not best pleased to be watching couture through 13 year old Tavi's hat'). Tavi's blog reply became the flashpoint of the 2010 editors-versus-bloggers backlash. A girl blocked the old guard's view, literally and figuratively.

media.search: Tavi Gevinson Stephen Jones bow Dior 2010 Hatgate
media.caption: Press photos (Paula Reed tweet photo; EPA via Independent). Copyrighted.

moments.title: Rookie launch — Prada lipstick skirt
moments.garments: Prada 'lipstick' skirt from spring 2010, hunted down on eBay, worn with bobby socks and black-and-white kilties.
moments.designer_season: Prada, spring 2010 collection (per Vanity Fair), bought second-hand on eBay.
moments.why_iconic: The Rookie-launch look. A teenager who had just started a feminist magazine wore a runway grail she tracked down second-hand, styled like a 1950s schoolgirl. It shows the resale instinct cool dairy is built on.

media.caption: Press photo. See Vanity Fair gallery.

moments.title: Met Gala 2016 — Coach 1941
moments.garments: Custom Coach 1941 short printed dress with collar, high neckline, pearl buttons, mixed prints. Black clutch, heeled sandals, red lipstick.
moments.designer_season: Custom Coach 1941 by Stuart Vevers (Teen Vogue; BoF).
moments.why_iconic: Six years after Hatgate, she walked the Met steps as a designer's guest. She still chose a wearable, collegiate, print-clash mini over a gown, a rejection of red-carpet formality.
